excerpt: Workers' compensation is a legally required insurance program, not an optional perk. What Georgia and South Carolina employers must provide.
keyTakeaways: Workers compensation is a legally mandated insurance program — not an optional employee benefit — that provides medical care and wage replacement for work-related injuries. Georgia requires coverage for employers with 3+ employees (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-1 et seq.), while South Carolina requires it for 4+ employees (S.C. Code § 42-1-10 et seq.). Benefits include TTD, TPD, PPD, medical treatment and death benefits, plus vocational rehabilitation in Georgia catastrophic cases. Filing deadlines are 1 year in Georgia (or 1 year after the last employer-paid treatment, or 2 years after the last income benefit, O.C.G.A. § 34-9-82) and 2 years in South Carolina.

faqs.question: Is workers compensation a benefit or a legal right?
faqs.answer: Workers compensation is a legally mandated insurance program, not a voluntary employee benefit. Both Georgia (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-1 et seq.) and South Carolina (S.C. Code § 42-1-10 et seq.) require qualifying employers to carry coverage. Unlike optional benefits like health insurance, workers comp is automatic, and employees cannot opt out of it (in Georgia, certain corporate officers and LLC members may exempt themselves under O.C.G.A. § 34-9-2.1).

faqs.question: Which employers are required to carry workers compensation in Georgia and South Carolina?
faqs.answer: In Georgia, employers with 3 or more employees must carry workers compensation insurance. In South Carolina, the threshold is 4 or more employees. Both full-time and part-time workers count toward these thresholds.

faqs.question: What benefits does workers compensation provide?
faqs.answer: Workers compensation provides medical benefits covering all authorized treatment, temporary total and partial disability benefits (typically two-thirds of average weekly wages, or of the wage difference for partial disability), permanent disability benefits, death benefits for surviving dependents, and — in Georgia catastrophic cases — vocational rehabilitation.

faqs.question: How long do I have to file a workers compensation claim?
faqs.answer: In Georgia, you must report the injury within 30 days and file a formal claim within 1 year of the injury, or within 1 year after the last employer-paid medical treatment or 2 years after the last weekly income benefit (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-82). In South Carolina, you must report within 90 days and file within 2 years (S.C. Code § 42-15-40). Missing these deadlines can jeopardize your benefits.

faqs.question: Are independent contractors covered by workers compensation?
faqs.answer: Generally, independent contractors are not covered by workers compensation. However, if you are misclassified as an independent contractor but actually function as an employee (set schedule, employer-provided tools, direct supervision), you may still qualify for benefits.

faqs.question: Can my employer fire me for filing a workers compensation claim in Georgia or South Carolina?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. In South Carolina, it is illegal to fire or demote you for filing a workers compensation claim in good faith; you can sue for lost wages and reinstatement, but you must do so within one year (S.C. Code § 41-1-80). Georgia has no equivalent law, and most employees there can be fired at will (Evans v. Bibb Co., 178 Ga. App. 139 (1986)), but losing your job does not necessarily end your benefits, especially if the firing was a pretext to avoid paying them (Padgett v. Waffle House, 269 Ga. 105 (1998)). An attorney can review your options in either state.

metaDescription: Workers' comp is required, not a perk: Georgia employers with 3+ workers and South Carolina employers with 4+ must carry it. Benefits and deadlines.
